@sujaykazi: The card moved in each step will be the one with the lowest label. Immediately after being moved, it will be the card with the highest label. The only inversions that can change as this card moves are those involving said card. Before the move, the number of inversions involving the card will be exactly the number of cards to the left of it in line (one inversion involving each). Likewise, the number of inversions will after the move be equal to the number of cards to the right of it in the line. By the definition of the process these two numbers are equal, and thus the number of inversions remains constant with each move.

Let each card begin as white, and suppose Karl paints each card black when he does the operation on it. For a card $c$ , define $f(c)$ as follows: - If $c$ is white, $f(c)$ equals the number of cards to the left of $c$ . - If $c$ is black, $f(c)$ equals the number of cards to the right of $c$ . [/list] We claim that, throughout the process, \[[\text{inverted pairs}] - \sum_{c \in \text{cards}} f(c)\] is invariant. This implies the problem. To show the quantity is invariant, note: [list] - If a black card gets shuffled one space left because of an operation, this means an inversion was created. If the black card is shuffled one space right, an inversion was deleted. - If a white card gets shuffled one space left, an inversion was deleted. If the white card is shuffled one space right, an inversion was created. [/list] In other words, when we shuffle cards in the middle left or right in an operation, these shuffles don't affect the invariant quantity. Moreover, the card that gets shuffled itself, by definition, maintains its quantity. So it is indeed invariant.

[rule] First, some definitions: Call a number changed/unchanged if Karl has done the reversing operation thing on it. Consider a number to be "shuffled around" when it is not the number being reversed, but one of the numbers whose position gets switched as a consequence. For example, if we go from 12345 to 13425, then, 3 and 4 got shuffled in that operation. Denote the "position" of a number to be $(\text{index from left}) - \frac{n+1}{2}$ if the number is unchanged, and $\frac{n+1}{2} - (\text{index from left})$ if the number is changed. Thus, the sum of the positions of all the numbers at the start and end of Karl's process is $0$ . When Karl reverses a number, it does not change the number's position. [rule] When an unchanged number gets shuffled left one index, this means that a number less than it has just been reversed, going from the left of that unchanged number to the right; this adds one inversion. So, an unchanged number getting shuffled left corresponds with one inversion being added - similarly, an unchanged number getting shuffled right one index corresponds with one inversion being removed. Oppositely, a changed number getting shuffled left one index corresponds with one inversion being removed, and a changed number getting shuffled right one index corresponds with one inversion being added. This can all be summarized by one rule: increasing the position of a number by $1$ decreases the number of inversions by $1$ , and decreasing the position of a number by $1$ increases the number of inversions by $1$ . But since the sum of the positions of all numbers starts and ends at $0$ , the total number of inversions added must total out to be $0$ as well. (I hope this solution is not a fakesolve. If it's indeed not a fakesolve, then I hope this solution is much more motivated than the solution provided by Evan Chen - this solution comes from trying to relate the position of numbers to the number of inversions, since the former is clearly invariant.)

For instance, in the problem given, this becomes \[ WWWW \longrightarrow WWBW \longrightarrow BWWB \longrightarrow BWBB \longrightarrow BBBB \] We claim then that the change in the number of inversions is the difference between the number of pairs $WB$ with a $W$ card preceeding a $B$ card by some number of cards, subtracting the pairs $BW$ . Then we can pair up the cards before and after the swapped card that aren't affected, as \[ WWW \mapsto WBW, WWB \mapsto WBB, BWW \mapsto BBW, BWB \mapsto BBB \] doesn't change the difference. Conversely, $WB \mapsto BB, WW \mapsto WB$ when moving a card on the left hand of the deck change the difference and number of inversions equally, and likewise. Since the difference is zero for all white and all black cards, the result follows.**Remark:** This also turns into the idea where you consider the sum of the positions of the moved cards, where adjacent positions differ by two and the signs are symmetric about the middle. Then the position invariant comes into play because you just flip a sign.

Color all the cards white initially, then switch the color to black after the card is moved. Observe the change in the number of swapped pairs each swap is the number of white cards to the left of a black card just after its swap minus the number of black cards on the right of the same black card that was white right before its swap.
Observe that if we sum the number of black cards to the right of each white card over all white cards as this process is iterated, we count each white card to the left of each black card exactly once. To prove this, choose a certain card that is black right after a swap. For each white card to its left, it will stay to its left until it is swapped. Therefore, as we sum each white card before it is swapped, every white card to its left will count this black card to its right exactly once in our sum. The counting of the other white cards does not affect this black card as they are either
\begin{itemize}
    \item To its right
    \item Or having been swapped to a black card before our card turned black, and thus were not considered in the swap.
\end{itemize}
Therefore, summing all the differences simply yields a change of  $0,$  so we are done.

stem_md: Find all functions  $f:(0,\infty) \rightarrow (0,\infty)$  such that \[f\left(x+\frac{1}{y}\right)+f\left(y+\frac{1}{z}\right) + f\left(z+\frac{1}{x}\right) = 1\] for all  $x,y,z >0$  with  $xyz =1$ .
solution_md:
EDITED 2018-04-23: some cleanup and filling in more details. As always, let $x=b/c$ , $y=c/a$ , $z=a/b$ (classical inequality trick). Then the problem becomes \[ \sum_{\text{cyc}} f\left( \frac{b+c}{a} \right) = 1. \] Let $f(t) = g(\frac{1}{t+1})$ , equivalently $g(s) = f(1/s-1)$ . Thus $g \colon (0,1) \to (0,1)$ which satisfies $\sum_{\text{cyc}} g\left( \frac{a}{a+b+c} \right) = 1$ , or equivalently \[ \boxed{g(a) + g(b) + g(c) = 1} \qquad \forall a+b+c=1. \] The rest of the solution is dedicated to solving this equivalent functional equation in $g$ . It is a lot of technical details and I will only outline them (with apologies to the contestants who didn't have that luxury).**Claim**: The function $g$ is linear. *Proof.* This takes several steps, all of which are technical. We begin by proving $g$ is linear over $(1/8, 3/8)$ . - First, whenever $a+b \le 1$ we have \[ 1 - g(1-(a+b)) = g(a) + g(b) = 2 g\left( \frac{a+b}{2} \right). \] Hence $g$ obeys Jensen's functional equation over $(0,1/2)$ . - Define $h \colon [0,1] \to {\mathbb R}$ by $h(t) = g(\frac{2t+1}{8}) - (1-t) \cdot g(1/8) - t \cdot g(3/8)$ , then $h$ satisfies Jensen's functional equation too over $[0,1]$ . We have also arranged that $h(0) = h(1) = 0$ , hence $h(1/2) = 0$ as well. - Since \[ h(t) = h(t) + h(1/2) = 2h(t/2+1/4) = h(t+1/2) + h(0) = h(t+1/2) \] for any $t < 1/2$ , we find $h$ is periodic modulo $1/2$ . It follows one can extend $\widetilde h$ by \[ \widetilde h \colon {\mathbb R} \to {\mathbb R} \qquad\text{by}\qquad \widetilde h(t) = h(t - \left\lfloor t \right\rfloor) \] and still satisfy Jensen's functional equation. Because $\widetilde h(0) = 0$ , it's well-known this implies $\widetilde h$ is additive (because $\widetilde h(x+y) = 2\widetilde h\left( (x+y)/2 \right) = \widetilde h(x) + \widetilde h(y)$ for any real numbers $x$ to $y$ ). But $\widetilde h$ is bounded below on $[0,1]$ since $g \ge 0$ , and since $\widetilde h$ is also additive, it follows (well-known) that $\widetilde h$ is linear. Hence so is $h$ . So, the function $g$ is linear over $(1/8,3/8)$ ; thus we may write $g(x) = kx + \ell$ , valid for $1/8 < x < 3/8$ . Since $3g(1/3) = 1$ , it follows $k + 3\ell = 1$ . For $0 < x < 1/8$ we have $g(x) = 2g(0.15) - g(0.3-x) = 2(0.15k+\ell) - (k(0.3-x)+\ell) = kx+\ell$ , so $g$ is linear over $(0,3/8)$ as well. Finally, for $3/8 < x < 1$ , we use the given equation \[ 1 = g\left( \frac{1-x}{2} \right) + g\left( \frac{1-x}{2} \right) + g(x) \implies g(x) = 1 - 2\left( k \cdot \frac{1-x}{2} + \ell \right) = kx+\ell \] since $\frac{1-x}{2} < \frac{5}{16} < \frac{3}{8}$ . Thus $g$ is linear over all. $\blacksquare$ Putting this back in, we deduce that $g(x) = kx + \frac{1-k}{3}$ for some $k \in [-1/2,1]$ , and so \[ f(x) = \frac{k}{x+1} + \frac{1-k}{3} \] for some $k \in [-1/2,1]$ . All such functions work.

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>By setting the first two terms to be  $a,b$ , we get the equation  $$ f(a)+f(b)+f\left(\dfrac{a+b+2}{ab-1}\right)=1.\,\,\,\,(1) $$  for all positive reals  $a,b$  with  $ab>1$ . Setting  $a=b>1$ , we get  $$ f\left(\dfrac{2}{a-1}\right)+2f(a)=1\,\,\,\,\, (2) $$  for all  $a>1$ . Our first main goal will be to prove that  $f(x)$  is continuous.

Define  $M:=\limsup\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x)=\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\sup\limits_{y>x}f(y)$ . For  $\epsilon>0$  small, pick  $K>1$  such that if  $x\geq K$ , then  $f(x)\leq M+\epsilon$ , and pick  $t>2K+1$  such that  $f(t)\geq M-\epsilon$ . Let  $y=\frac{2}{t-1}<\frac{1}{K}$ , and then from equation (2),  $$ f(y)=1-2f(t)\leq 1-2(M-\epsilon). $$  Let  $a=y,b>\frac{1}{y},z=\frac{a+b+2}{ab-1}$  (so  $ab>1$ ), and equation (1) implies that  $f(y)+f(b)+f(z)=1$ . As  $y<\frac{1}{K}$ , we see that  $b>K$ , whence  $f(b)\leq M+\epsilon$ . Thus  $$ f(z)=1-f(y)-f(b)\geq 1-(1-2(M-\epsilon))-(M+\epsilon)=M-3\epsilon. $$  We can take any  $b$  in the range  $(\frac{1}{y},\infty)$ , and in this range  $z$  ranges from  $\infty$  to  $\frac{1}{a}=\frac{t-1}{2}$ . In particular, this implies that for any  $\epsilon>0$ , there exists a positive real number  $K_{\epsilon}$  such that  $$ x>K_{\epsilon}\Leftrightarrow M-\epsilon \leq f(x)\leq M+\epsilon. $$  This statement essentially translates to  $f(x)$  is continuous at  $\infty$ .

Now, take any  $x$ , small  $\epsilon>0$ , and small  $\alpha$  (possibly negative), where  $\alpha$  is small enough so that  $(\frac{1}{x}+\epsilon)(x+\alpha)>1$  (this will be true for  $\alpha$  sufficiently small in magnitude). Apply equation (1) to the pairs  $(a,b)=(x,\frac{1}{x}+\epsilon),(\frac{1}{x}+\epsilon,x+\alpha)$ :
\begin{align*}
f(x)+f\left(\dfrac{1}{x}+\epsilon\right)+f\left(\dfrac{x+\frac{1}{x}+\epsilon+2}{\epsilon x}\right)= & 1
f(x+\alpha)+f\left(\dfrac{1}{x}+\epsilon\right)+f\left(\dfrac{x+\frac{1}{x}+\epsilon+\alpha+2}{\epsilon x+\frac{\alpha}{x}+\alpha\epsilon}\right)= & 1.
\end{align*}
For a fixed sufficiently small  $\epsilon$  and  $\alpha$  varying over a small range containing  $0$ , we can make the third term inside the function in each sum be as large as we like; make it bigger than  $K_{\delta}$ , some fixed  $\delta$  small. Therefore the term is within  $\delta$  of  $M$ , and subtracting the two equations we derive  $$ |f(x+\alpha)-f(x)|\leq 2\delta $$  for any small enough  $\delta$ . This is valid for any  $\delta>0$ , and sufficiently small  $\alpha$  (depending on  $\delta$ ), and thus  $f(x)$  is continuous everywhere.

To finish, we need a couple more equations. In equation (1), fix  $a=x$  and take  $b=\frac{1}{x}+\epsilon$  for  $\epsilon>0$ . Sending  $\epsilon\rightarrow 0$ , the third term tends to  $M$  and the second to  $f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$  by continuity. Therefore we get  $$ f(x)+f\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)=1-M\,\,\,\,\, (3) $$  for all  $x$ . Taking equation (2) and inverting the first term gives us   $$ 2f(x)=M+f\left(\dfrac{x-1}{2}\right)\,\,\,\,\, (4) $$  for  $x>1$ .
From this and equation (1), we can derive equalities like  $$ f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=\dfrac{2}{3}-M,\,\,\, f(1)=\dfrac{1-M}{2},\,\,\,f(2)=\dfrac{1}{3},\,\, f(3)=\dfrac{M+1}{4}. $$  In particular, we note that all of these equalities take the form  $$ f(x)=\dfrac{(x-2)M+1}{x+1}. $$  Note that this is a valid solution as long as  $0\leq M<\frac{1}{2}$ .

To prove this equation holds true for all  $x$ , let  $f(x)-\dfrac{(x-2)M+1}{x+1}=\epsilon_x$ . Equation (4) tells us that  $\epsilon_{(x-1)/2}=2\epsilon_x$  for all  $x>1$ . Equation (3) tells us that  $\epsilon_{\frac{1}{x}}=-\epsilon_{x}$ . Thus if we start with an  $x$  satisfying  $\epsilon_x\neq 0$ , apply the two operations  $$ x\Rightarrow \dfrac{x-1}{2}\text{ if  $x>1$ },x\Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{x}\text{ if  $x<1$ } $$  and if we can apply these in perpetuity the magnitude of  $\epsilon_x$  will grow to be arbitrarily large, contradiction. The only way that we cannot apply this forever would be if we eventually land on  $x=1$ , but  $\epsilon_1=0$  so we are done.
Thus  $\epsilon_x=0$  for all  $x$ , completing the problem.</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Pretty much what I submitted word for word, except the parts that say "as v_Enhance did" I actually wrote out. 

We claim that all solutions are the functions of the form  $f(x) = cx + \frac{1-c}{3}$ , for  $c \in [-\frac{1}{2}, 1]$ .

By plugging we can check that these work.

Now, we will show that they are all solutions.

Let  $g(s) = f(1/s-1),$  as v_Enhance did, to reduce it to the functional equation:

\[ {g(a) + g(b) + g(c) = 1} \qquad \forall a+b+c=1. \]

Note that  $g$  has a domain and range of  $(0,1)$ .

Claim.  $g$  is linear. $\newline$ Proof. As v_Enhance noted, 

\[ 1-g(1-a-b) = g(a) + g(b) = 2g(\frac{a+b}{2}). \]

In order to get that  $g(a) + g(b) = 2g(\frac{a+b}{2})$  for all  $a, b \in (0, 1)$  (i.e. not just for  $a+b < 1$ ), we just do it for  $\frac{1-a}{2}, \frac{1-b}{2}$  and observe that  $g(a) = 1-2g(\frac{1-a}{2}))$ , etc.

Therefore, we actually get that:

\[ g(a) + g(b) = 2g(\frac{a+b}{2})\],

for all  $a, b \in (0,1)$ .

Thus, arithmetic sequences map to arithmetic sequences.

In other words, 

\[ g(a+b) - g(a) = g(a+2b) - g(a+b) = \cdots = g(a+kb) - g(a+(k-1)b), (1)\]

for any real a, b so that  $a, a+b, \cdots, a+kb$  are all in (0, 1).

From here, we obtain that  $g$  is linear over the rationals. 

To see this, note that any rational other than  $\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{3}$  is in an arithmetic progression with  $\frac{1}{2}$  and  $\frac{1}{3}$ . 
For instance, if it had denominator  $d$  then take the arithmetic progression  $\frac{1}{6d}, \frac{2}{6d}, \cdots, \frac{6d-1}{6d}$ .

Let  $a, b$  be such that  $g(q) = aq+b,$  for all rational  $q$ .

Now, we will show that  $g(x) = ax+b$  for all  $x \in (0, 1)$ .

Sketch. Assume that some irrational  $x$  does not satisfy that.

Let's first see what happens if  $g(x) < ax+b$ .

Then take a rational  $q$  with  $x> q > x- \epsilon$ , for  $\epsilon$  to be specified later.

This can be done for all  $\epsilon$  by the density of the rationals.

The idea is that by looking at the arithmetic sequence with starting term  $f(q)$  and common difference  $f(x) - f(q)$ , some term of it will eventually be negative because of how small  $g(x)$  is.

This was slightly hard to rigorize, but you get the idea.

In the case that  $g(x) > ax+b$ , you do the exact same thing, and you can get a value mapping to  $>1$ . $\blacksquare$ Now you pretty much win and plug in. :D

Here is another proof which is using usual method of proving for rationals and moving to reals using continuity.
After plugging  $(x, y, z) = \left(\frac{a}{b}, \frac{b}{c}, \frac{c}{a}\right)$  and defining  $g(x): (0, 1) \to (0, 1)$  as  $g(x):=f\left(\frac{1}{x} - 1\right)$  we get  $$ g(a) + g(b) + g(c) = 1 $$  for all  $0< a, b, c < 1$  such that  $a+b+c =1$ . Our goal is to prove that  $$ g(x) = x + (1 - 3x)\cdot C $$  for some constant  $C$ . 
If  $a=b=c = \frac{1}{3}$ , then  $g\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{3}$ . By changing  $(a, b)$  with  $(a + (j-1)b, b)$  and  $(a + (j-2)b, 2b)$  we get  $$ g(a + (j-1)b) - g(a+(j-2)b) = g(2b) - g(b) $$  for all  $a, b > 0$  and integer  $j\geq 2$  such that  $a + jb < 1$ . Summing this for  $j=2, 3, \dots, k$  we get
\begin{align*}
g(a + (k-1)b) = (k-1)(g(2b) - g(b)) + g(a)
\end{align*}
for all  $a, b > 0$  and  $k\in \mathbb{N}$  such that  $a + kb < 1$ . In particular, we have  $$ g(kb) = (k-1)(g(2b) - g(b)) + g(b) $$  Let  $n\geq 3$  be an integer and plug  $b = \frac{1}{n}$  in the last equation to get
\begin{align*}
g\left(\frac{k}{n}\right) = (k-1)\left(g\left(\frac{2}{n}\right) - g\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\right) + g\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)  \qquad\qquad (2)
\end{align*}
for all integers  $1 \leq k \leq n-2$ . Let  $(a, b, c) = \left(\frac{1}{n}, \frac{1}{n}, \frac{n-2}{n}\right)$  in the main equation to get  $$ 1 = g\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) + g\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)+ g\left(\frac{n-2}{n}\right)= (n-3)\left(g\left(\frac{2}{n}\right) - g\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\right) + 3g\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) $$  So by multiplying both sides of  $(2)$  by  $n-3$  we get  $$ (n-3)g\left(\frac{k}{n}\right) = (k-1) + (n-3k)g\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) $$  Let   $$ g(x) = x + (1 - 3x)h(x) $$  and plug this into above equation to get  $$ h\left(\frac{k}{n}\right) = h\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) $$  for all  $n\geq 4$  and  $1\leq k \leq n-2$  such that  $n\neq 3k$ . Then for all  $n\geq 4$   $$ h\left(\frac{1}{n}\right) = h\left(\frac{2}{2n}\right) = h\left(\frac{n}{2n}\right) = h\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) $$     
Note that since  $g\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{3}$  we can define  $h\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) := h\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$ . \[g(a)+g(b)+g(c) = 1\]
Note that for  $a,b<\frac12$ ,  $g$  satisfies 
\[g(a)+g(b) = 1-g(1-a-b) = 2\cdot g(\frac{a+b}{2})\]
Thus,  $g$  satisfies Jensens on the range  $(0,\frac12)$ . Now consider  $h$ , the difference between  $g(t)$  for  $t\in [\alpha,\beta]$  and the line between  $g(\alpha)$  and  $g(\beta)$ , where  $0< \alpha < \frac32 \alpha <  \beta < \frac12$  and  $\beta > \frac13$  (this is easily gotten by choosing  $\alpha=\epsilon_1$  and  $\beta = \frac12 -\epsilon_2$ . This  $h:[0,1]\to (0,1)$  is formally defined as 
\[h(t) = g(\alpha + t(\beta -\alpha) ) - (1-t) \cdot g(\alpha) - t\cdot g(\beta)\]
This clearly satisfies  $h(0)=h(1)=1$ . Additionally, note that  $g$  is Jensen in the range  $[\alpha,\beta]$ , and thus Jensen for all  $h(t)$ . Thus,  $h(\frac12) = \frac12 (h(0)+h(1)) = 0$ , and we also have that  $h$  is periodic mod  $\frac12$ :
\[h(t+\frac12) = \frac12 (h(2t)+h(1)) = \frac12 (2h(t)-h(0)+h(1)) = h(t)\]
Then, extend  $h$  to be defined for all  $t$ , where  $h(t) = h(t-\lfloor t\rfloor)$ . 

Then, Jensen's still holds since in the following equation shifting  $x+y$  down by 1 shifts  $\frac{x+y}{2}$  down by  $\frac12$ , which is still invariant on both sides. (and for the second equation, shifting  $x$  or  $y$  down by 1, also changes  $\frac{x+y}{2}$  by  $\frac12$ , which is invariant due to the periodicity).
\[h(0) + h(x+y) = 2 h(\frac{x+y}{2})  = h(x) + h(y) \]
We have  $h(0)=0$ , so we have additivity, and  $h(x)\geq 0$ , which is well known to imply that  $h$  is linear. Since  $h(0)=h(1)=0$ , this means that  $h(t)$  for all  $t$ , and thus  $g(x)$  is linear for  $x\in [\alpha,\beta]$ . Write this as  $g(x) = AX+B$ .

Next, consider  $x\in (0,\alpha]$ . We have that (since  $\frac12 x + \alpha < \frac32 \alpha <\beta$ )
\[g(x) = 2 g(\frac12 x + \alpha) - g(2 \alpha) = 2 \cdot (A(\frac12 x + \alpha) + B) - 2A\cdot \alpha - B=Ax+B \]
Thus,  $g(x) = Ax+B$  for  $x\in (0,\alpha] \cup [\alpha,\beta] = (0,\beta]$ .

Note that since  $\beta>\frac13$ , we have  $\frac13\in [\alpha,\beta]$  and thus  $1 = 3g(\frac13) = A+3B$ . Penultimately, consider  $x\in [\beta,\frac12)$ . These satisfy
\[2g(x) = 1- g(1-2x) = 1- A(1-2x) -B = A+3B - A + 2xA - B = 2xA + 2B\]
where  $1-2x < \frac13< \beta$  since  $\beta > \frac13$ , and this implies  $g(x) = Ax + B$ .

Finally, consider  $x\in [\frac12, 1)$ . Then,
\[g(x) = 1- g(b) - g(c) = A+3B - Ab - B - Ac - B = Ax + B\]
since  $x+b+c=1$ , and  $b,c < 1-x < \frac12$ .

Thus,  $g$  is always linear and equal to  $AX+B$ . Returning to the  $a+b+c=1\Longrightarrow g(a)+g(b)+g(c)=1$ , this is always satisfied as long as  $A+3B=1$ . But not all  $A$  are valid, we must also have  $AX+B\geq 0$  for all  $x\in [0,1]$ . Since this is linear, we only need to verify  $0+B\geq 0$  and  $A+B\geq 0$ . Thus,  $1 = A+3B \geq 2B$ , so  $B\leq \frac12$ . Thus, the range of  $B$  is  $[0,\frac12]$ , and the range of  $A$  is  $[-\frac12, 1]$ , paired so that  $A+3B=1$ .  $\blacksquare$ .

stem_md:
For a given integer  $n\ge 2$ , let  $\{a_1,a_2,…,a_m\}$  be the set of positive integers less than  $n$  that are relatively prime to  $n$ . Prove that if every prime that divides  $m$  also divides  $n$ , then  $a_1^k+a_2^k + \dots + a_m^k$  is divisible by  $m$  for every positive integer  $k$ . 

*Proposed by Ivan Borsenco*
solution_md:
Let a number  $n \ge 1$  be *stable* if every prime dividing  $\phi(n)$  also divides  $n$ . First, we classify all stable  $n$  in a different way:**Classification.**  $n$  is stable if and only if for all primes  $p$  and  $q$  with  $p \mid n$  and  $q \mid p - 1$  we have  $q \mid n$ .

*Proof.* Suppose  $n$  is stable,  $p \mid n$ ,  $q \mid p - 1$ , and  $q \nmid n$ . Then  $q$  divides  $\phi(n)$  but not  $n$ , contradiction. Conversely, it is easy to see if  $n$  satisfies this property, it is stable.  $\blacksquare$ **Corollary 1.** If  $n > 1$  is stable and  $p$  is the largest prime divisor of  $n$ , then  $n/p$  is stable.**Corollary 2.** If  $n > 1$  is stable, there exists a chain  $x_0 = 1 \mid x_1 \mid x_2 \mid \cdots \mid x_k = n$  of stable numbers such that  $x_r/x_{r-1}$  is the largest prime factor of each  $x_r$ . As an example, for  $n = 342 = 2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 19$  we have the stable chain
\[1 \mid 2 \mid 6 \mid 18 \mid 342.\]
-----
The proof is in two parts: handling squarefree stable  $n$ , then extending to all stable  $n$ . Extending from squarefree  $n$  to all  $n$  is easier and independent of the first part, but we present it second to make the flow natural.

First we handle squarefree stable  $n$ . We proceed by induction on  $n$  with base cases  $n \le 2$  trivial.

Let  $n$  be stable and  $p$  a prime not dividing  $n$  such that  $pn$  is also stable. Let  $m = \phi(n)$ , let  $a_1, \dots, a_m$  be the [url = https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totative]totatives[/url] of  $n$ , and  $b_1, \dots, b_{(p-1)m}$  be those of  $pn$ . Thus we assume
\[m \mid a_1^k + \dots + a_m^k\]
for all  $k$  and wish to prove
\[(p - 1)m \mid b_1^k + \dots + b_{(p - 1)m}^k\]
for all  $k$ . It is enough to check the latter divisibility for each prime divisor  $q$  of  $(p - 1)m$ . Since  $pn$  is stable, each prime divisor  $q$  of  $(p - 1)m$  also divides  $pn$ ; by assumption  $p \nmid m$ , so  $q \mid n$ .

The key insight is that the numbers  $b_1, \dots, b_{(p - 1)m}$  are exactly the numbers
\begin{tabular}{cccc} $a_1$  &  $a_2$  &  $\dots$  &  $a_m$  $a_1 + n$  &  $a_2 + n$  &  $\dots$  &  $a_m + n$  $\vdots$  &  $\vdots$  &  $\ddots$  &  $\vdots$  $a_1 + (p - 1)n$  &  $a_2 + (p - 1)n$  &  $\dots$  &  $a_m + (p - 1)n$ \end{tabular}
excluding  $pa_1, \dots, pa_m$ . Hence
\[\sum_{i = 1}^{(p - 1)m} b_i^k = \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 0}^{p - 1} (a_i + jn)^k - p^k \sum_{i = 1}^{m} a_i^k.\]
Let  $s_k = a_1^k + \dots + a_m^k$  for conciseness, so
\[\sum_{i = 1}^{(p - 1)m} b_i^k = \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 0}^{p - 1} (a_i + jn)^k - p^k s_k.\]

Let  $q$  be a prime divisor of  $(p - 1)m$  (and also of  $n$ ). We must show
\[\nu_q \left(\sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 0}^{p - 1} (a_i + jn)^k - p^k s_k\right) \ge \nu_q((p - 1)m).\]
Suppose  $q \nmid p - 1$ . Then the expression  $\sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 0}^{p - 1} (a_i + jn)^k - p^k s_k$  is an integer combination of expressions of the form  $s_{\ell}$ , so it is divisible by  $m$  and thus
\[\nu_q \left(\sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 0}^{p - 1} (a_i + jn)^k - p^k s_k\right) \ge \nu_q(m) = \nu_q((p - 1)m)\]
as desired.

Now suppose  $q \mid p - 1$ . Recall that we wish to show the number
\[\sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 0}^{p - 1} (a_i + jn)^k - p^k s_k = \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 1}^{p - 1} (a_i + jn)^k - (p^k - 1) s_k\]
is divisible by  $q^{\nu_q(p - 1) + \nu_q(m)}$ .

The term  $(p^k - 1) s_k$  is a multiple of  $(p - 1)m$ , which is a multiple of  $q^{\nu_q(p - 1) + \nu_q(m)}$ . The other term rewrites as
\begin{align*}
\sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 1}^{p - 1} (a_i + jn)^k & = \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 1}^{p - 1} \left(a_i^k + \binom{k}{1} a_i^{k - 1} jn + \dots + \binom{k}{k} (jn)^k\right)
& = \sum_{j = 1}^{p - 1} \left(s_k + \binom{k}{1} s_{k - 1} jn + \dots + \binom{k}{k} s_0 (jn)^k\right).
\end{align*}
We show that each term
\[\binom{k}{r} s_{k - r} (1^r + \dots + (p - 1)^r) n^r\]
is a multiple of  $q^{\nu_q(p - 1) + \nu_q(m)}$ . Note that  $s_{k - r}$  is a multiple of  $m$ , so it is enough to show
\[\nu_q(1^r + \dots + (p - 1)^r) + \nu_q(n^r) \ge \nu_q(p - 1).\]
Note that  $1^r + \dots + (p - 1)^r$  is  $\tfrac{p - 1}{r!}$  times an integer. Recall  $q \mid n$ , and we get
\[\nu_q(1^r + \dots + (p - 1)^r) + \nu_q(n^r) \ge \nu_q(p - 1) - \nu_q(r!) + r \ge \nu_q(p - 1)\]
as desired. This shows that  $(p - 1)m$  divides  $b_1^k + \dots + b_{(p - 1)m}^k$ , completing the induction.
-----
Now, we extend from  $n$  squarefree stable to all stable  $n$ . Let  $p$  be a prime divisor of a stable  $n$  (so  $pn$  is also stable). Letting  $a_1, \dots, a_m$  denote the totatives of  $n$ , the totatives  $b_1, \dots, b_{pm}$  of  $pn$  are exactly the numbers
\begin{tabular}{cccc} $a_1$  &  $a_2$  &  $\dots$  &  $a_m$  $a_1 + n$  &  $a_2 + n$  &  $\dots$  &  $a_m + n$  $\vdots$  &  $\vdots$  &  $\ddots$  &  $\vdots$  $a_1 + (p - 1)n$  &  $a_2 + (p - 1)n$  &  $\dots$  &  $a_m + (p - 1)n$ \end{tabular}
Let  $n = pt$ , so these totatives are
\begin{tabular}{cccc} $a_1$  &  $a_2$  &  $\dots$  &  $a_m$  $a_1 + pt$  &  $a_2 + pt$  &  $\dots$  &  $a_m + pt$  $\vdots$  &  $\vdots$  &  $\ddots$  &  $\vdots$  $a_1 + (p - 1)pt$  &  $a_2 + (p - 1)pt$  &  $\dots$  &  $a_m + (p - 1)pt$ \end{tabular}
Hence we must show  $pm$  divides  $\sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 0}^{p - 1} (a_i + jpt)^k$ . This rewrites as\begin{align*}
\sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 0}^{p - 1} (a_i + jpt)^k & = \sum_{i = 1}^{m} \sum_{j = 0}^{p - 1} \left(a_i^k + \binom{k}{1} a_i^{k - 1} jpt + \dots + \binom{k}{k} (jpt)^k\right)
& = \sum_{j = 0}^{p - 1} \left(s_k + \binom{k}{1} s_{k - 1} jpt + \dots + \binom{k}{k} s_0 (jpt)^k\right).
\end{align*}
The  $s_k$  terms coalesce into  $ps_k$ , which is a multiple of  $pm$ . The remaining terms
\[\binom{k}{r} s_{k - r} (1^r + \dots + (p - 1)^r) p^r n^r\]
are multiples of  $pm$  for  $r \ge 1$ . Thus  $pm$  divides  $b_1^k + \dots + b_{pm}^k$ . By induction, the problem is solved for all stable  $n$ .

For brevity, given any  $n$ , we let  $A(n) = \left\{ 1 \le x \le n, \gcd(x,n) = 1 \right\}$  (thus  $\# A(n) = \varphi(n)$ ). Also, let  $S(n,k) = \sum_{a \in A(n)} a^k$ .

We will prove the stronger statement (which eliminates the hypothesis on  $n$ ).**Claim**:  	Let  $n \ge 2$  be arbitrary (and  $k \in {\mathbb Z}$ ). 	If  $p \mid n$ , then \[ \nu_p (\varphi(n)) \le \nu_p(S(n,k)). \]

We start with the special case where  $n$  is a prime power.**Lemma**:  	We always have 	\[ S(p^e) = \sum_{x \in A(p^e)} x^k \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{e-1}}.  \]

*Proof.*  	For  $p$  odd, this follows by taking a primitive root modulo  $p^{e-1}$ . 	In the annoying case  $p = 2$ , the proof is broken into two cases: 	for  $k$  odd it follows by pairing  $x$  with  $2^e-x$  	and when  $k$  is even one can take  $5$  as a generator 	and do a similar proof as in the first case.  $\blacksquare$ **Corollary**:  	We have  $\nu_p(1^k + \dots + t^k) \ge \nu_p(t) - 1$  for any  $k$ , 	 $t$ ,  $p$ .

*Proof.*  	Assume  $p \mid t$ . 	Discard the terms in that sum divisible by  $p$  	and apply the lemma a bunch of times.  $\blacksquare$ Now the idea is to add primes  $q$  one at a time to  $n$ , starting from the base case  $n = p^e$ . So, formally we proceed by induction on the number of prime divisors of  $n$ .

 
- First, suppose we want to go from  $n$  to  $nq$  where  $q \nmid n$ . In that case  $\varphi(nq)$  gained  $\nu_p(q-1)$  factors of  $p$  and then we need to show  $\nu_p(S(nq,k)) \ge \nu_p(\varphi(n)) + \nu_p(q-1)$ . The trick is to write \[ A(nq) = \left\{ a + nh \mid a \in A(n) 		\text{ and } h = 0,\dots,q-1 \right\} 		\setminus qA(n)  \] and then expand using binomial theorem: \begin{align*} 	S(nq, k) &= 	\sum_{a \in A(n)} \sum_{h=0}^{q-1} (a+nh)^k 	- \sum_{a \in A(n)} (qa)^k  	&= \sum_{j=0}^k  \sum_{a \in A(n)} \sum_{h=0}^{q-1}\binom kj a^{k-j} 		(nh)^j - q^k S(n,k)  	&= \sum_{j=0}^k \sum_{h=1}^{q-1} S(n,k-j) \binom kj n^j h^j 		- q^k S(n,k)  	&= (q-q^k) S(n,k) 		+ \sum_{j=1}^k S(n,k-j) \binom kj n^j 		\sum_{h=1}^{q-1} h^j. \end{align*} We claim every term here has enough powers of  $p$ . For the first term,  $S(n,k)$  has at least  $\nu_p(\varphi(n))$  factors of  $p$ ; and we have the  $q-q^k$  multiplier out there. For the other terms, we apply induction to  $S(n,k-j)$ ; moreover  $\sum_{h=1}^{q-1} h^j$  has at least  $\nu_p(q-1)-1$  factors of  $p$  by corollary, and we get one more factor of  $p$  (at least) from  $n^j$ .
- On the other hand, if  $q$  already divides  $n$ , then this time \[ A(nq) = \left\{ a + nh \mid a \in A(n) 		\text{ and } h = 0,\dots,q-1 \right\}.  \] and we have no additional burden of  $p$  to deal with; the same calculation gives \[ S(nq,k) = qS(n,k) 	+ \sum_{j=1}^k S(n,k-j) \binom kj n^j 	\sum_{h=1}^{q-1} h^j. \] which certainly has enough factors of  $p$  already.

<details><summary>Solution</summary>First, prove for prime products. By induction on  $s$ , where  $n = p_1 p_2 \dots p_s$ . Oh first define  $A(n)$  to be set of positive integers less than, relatively prime to  $n$ . Clearly  $|A| = \phi(n) = \prod_{i=1}^s (p_i - 1)$ . Also say  $n$  is good if prime  $p \mid \phi(n)$  implies  $p \mid n$ . We only consider good  $n$ .

Base case  $s = 1$  is trivial:  $\phi(n)$  and  $n$  are relatively prime, so they can't share prime factor, imply  $m = 1$  and trivial.

Suppose true for  $s-1$ . Consider  $n = p_1 p_2 \dots p_s$ , WLOG  $p_1 < p_2 < \dots < p_s$ . It's good, so  $p \mid \phi(n) \rightarrow p \mid n$ . But  $p_s \nmid \phi(n)$  since it's too big, so  $p \mid \frac{n}{p_s}$ . Hence,  $\frac{n}{p_s}$  is good, and we can apply inductive hypothesis: if  $P = p_1 p_2 \dots p_{s-1}$ , then  $$ \phi(P) \mid \sum_{a \in A(P)} a^k $$  for all  $k$ . Let  $p = p_s$  for convenience. We have  $\phi(n) = (p-1) \phi(P)$ . Also  $A(n)$  is formed by adding either  $0, P, 2P, \dots, (p-1)P$  to  $A(P)$ , and subtracting  $p$  times any number in  $A(P)$ . Thus, it suffices to prove  $$ (p-1) \phi(P) \mid \left( \sum_{a \in A(P)} \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} (a + iP)^k \right) - \sum_{a \in A(P)} (pa)^k. $$  Note that  $$ (p-1) \phi(P) \mid (p^k - p) \sum_{a \in A(P)} a^k $$  ( $p-1$  divides the first term in the product, while  $\phi(P)$  divides the summation), and for  $1 \le j \le k$ ,  $$ \sum_{a \in A(P)} \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} \binom{k}{j} a^{k-j} (iP)^j = \binom{k}{j} P^j \left( \sum_{a \in A(P)} a^{k-j} \right) \left( \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} i^j \right). $$  The first parenthesis product is divisible by  $\phi(P)$ , so it suffices to prove  $$ p-1 \mid P \sum_{i=0}^{p-1} i^j. $$  Since any prime factor of  $p-1$  divides  $P$ , it suffices to prove  $$ q^{t-1} \mid \sum_{i=0}^{a \cdot q^t} i^j $$  for any  $t \ge 2$ . This is by induction on  $t$ ; base case trivial, inductive step is  $$ \sum_{i=0}^{a \cdot q^t} i^j \equiv aq \sum_{i=0}^{q^{t-1}} i^j \equiv 0 \pmod {q^{t-1}}. $$  Now iterate over all  $1 \le j \le k$ , and add the divisibilities and use the Binomial theorem to prove the result for prime products.

Extending from prime products to prime powers isn't hard. We claim if  $p \mid n$  and  $n$  works, then  $np$  works. Indeed,  $\phi(np) = p \phi(n)$ , and  $A(np)$  is formed by adding either  $0, n, 2n, \dots, (p-1)n$  to each element of  $A(n)$ . Now we use a similar Binomial theorem argument (except easier) to finish. (And this last part I was able to do during the test; hoping for minimal partial.)</details>

This problem is a lot similar to a problem that I proposed and appeared in the September 2017 competition of the Bulgarian magazine "Mathematics." 

My problem states:

Prove that there exists a function $f:N \longrightarrow N$ , such that for every pair of positive integers  $n$  and  $k$ ,   $$ \varphi(n) / f(k)(a_1^k+a_2^k+...a_{\varphi(n)}^k). $$   
The integers  $a_1,a_2,...a_{\varphi(n)}$  are the positive integers less than  $n$   and coprime with  $n$ .

Though the problem is different, it is easy to check that with slight modifications the solution would work also for the USAMO problem.**Solution:**We begin with the following Lemma:**Lemma:** For every nonnegative integer k there exists a polynomial  $P_k$  with rational coefficients, such that $P_k(0)=0$ ,   $P_k(n)=1^k+2^k+...n^k$ , and  $deg(P_k)=k+1$ .
We will prove the statement by induction. 

1)Base:  $k=0$ , obviously  $P_0(n)=n$ Step: We will prove it for  $k=t+1$ . Consider the following equality:   $$ (1+x)^{t+2}=\sum_{a=0}^{t+2} {{{t+2}\choose{a}}x^a}. $$   Now we make all these equalities for  $1 \le x \le n$  and add them. We obtain the expression:
\begin{eqnarray*}
2^{t+2}+3^{t+2}+...(n+1)^{t+2}=\sum_{a=0}^{t+2} {{t+2}\choose{a}}(1^a+2^a+....n^a)=
 =\sum_{a=0}^{t} {{t+2}\choose{a}} P_a(n)+(t+1)(1^{t+1}+2^{t+1}+...n^{t+1})+(1^{t+2}+2^{t+2}+...n^{t+2}).
\end{eqnarray*} Subtracting some terms on both sides, we have:  $$ (n+1)^{t+2}-1-\sum_{a=0}^{t} {{t+2}\choose{a}} P_a(n)=(t+1)(1^{t+1}+...+n^{t+1}). $$   

This means that   $$ \displaystyle P_{t+1}(n)=\frac{(n+1)^{t+2}-1-\sum_{a=0}^{t} {{t+2}\choose{a}} P_a(n)}{t+1}, $$  and  the **Lemma** follows.


Now, having the **Lemma**, we are going back to the original problem. 

Let   $$ \displaystyle P_k(x)=\sum_{a=1}^{k+1} \alpha_{k+1-a}x^a. $$   We will prove that if we choose  $f(k)$  to be such a positive integer that  $f(k) \alpha_i$  is an integer for every  $0 \le i \le k$  the condition will hold.

Let   $n$  has the form  $n=p_1^{\alpha_1}p_2^{\alpha_2}...p_r^{\alpha_r}$ . If  $gcd(n,x)>1$ , there exists a prime nuber  $p$ , such that  $p/gcd(n,x)$ . So we will do a PIE on the set of different primes dividing  $gcd(x,n)$ . 

We have that the sum of  $k$ th powers of the integers less than  $n$  and divisible by  $Q$ , where  $Q/p_1p_2...p_r$  is   $$  (Q^k+(2Q)^k+...(n)^k)=Q^kP_k(\frac{n}{Q}). $$   Now using PIE, we have that:

\begin{eqnarray*}
f(k)(a_1^k+a_2^k+...a_{\varphi(n)}^k)=f(k)(\sum_{Q/p_1p_2...p_r} Q^kP_k(\frac{n}{Q})\mu(Q))=
 =f(k)(\sum_{Q/p_1p_2...p_r}(\sum_{a=1}^{k+1}\alpha_{k+1-a} n^a Q^{k-a}\mu(Q))=A
\end{eqnarray*}

But it is easy to show that   $$ \sum_{Q/p_1p_2...p_r} Q^x\mu(Q)=(1-p_1^x)(1-p_2^x)...(1-p_r^x). $$   

So   $$ A=\sum_{a=1}^{k+1} f(k)\alpha_{k+1-a}n^{a}(1-p_1^{k-a})(1-p_2^{k-a})...(1-p_r^{k-a}). $$  But since when  $n=p_1^{\alpha_1}p_2^{\alpha_2}...p_r^{\alpha_r}$ ,

\begin{eqnarray*}
\varphi(n)=n(1-p_1^{-1})(1-p_2^{-1})...(1-p_r^{-1})=
 =(p_1-1)(p_2-1)...(p_r-1)p_1^{\alpha_1-1}p_2^{\alpha_2-1}...p_r^{\alpha_r-1}/(1-p_1^{a-1})(1-p_2^{a-1})...(1-p_r^{a-1})n,
\end{eqnarray*} the result follows.

For any positive integer  $n \ge 2$  let  $S_n$  be the set of positive integers less than  $n$  that are relatively prime to  $n$ , and for any set  $S$  let  $$ \Sigma(S, k) = \sum_{s \in S} s^k $$  We wish to prove that if any prime dividing  $\phi(n)$  divides  $n$  then  $\phi(n) \mid \Sigma(S_n, k)$  for any positive integer  $k$ . We first reduce the problem to the case when  $n$  is squarefree. Namely we prove that if  $n$  works and  $p$  is a prime divisor of  $n$  then  $np$  works too. Notice that  $\phi(np) = p\phi(n)$ , and that  $S_{np} = \{s + in \vert s \in S_n, 0 \leq i \leq p - 1\}$ . Therefore  $$ \Sigma(S_{np}, k) = \sum_{s \in S_n}\sum_{i = 0}^{p - 1} (s + in)^k = \sum_{s \in S}\sum_{i = 0}^{p - 1}\sum_{j = 0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}s^j(in)^{k - j} = \sum_{j = 0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}\left(\sum_{i = 0}^{p - 1} (in)^{k - j}\right)\left(\sum_{s \in S_n} s^j\right) = \sum_{j = 0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}\left(\sum_{i = 0}^{p - 1}(in)^{k - j}\right)\Sigma(S_n, j) $$  Now if  $q \mid \phi(n)$  then by hypothesis  $q^{v_q(\phi(n))} \mid \Sigma(S_n, j)$ , and therefore the entire sum is divisible by  $q^{v_q(\phi(n))}$ . It remains to prove that we have an additional factor when  $q = p$ . It evidently suffices to prove that  $p$  divides  $\displaystyle\sum_{i = 0}^{p - 1}(in)^{k - j}$  for any  $j \in [0, k]$ . If  $j \neq k$  then  $n$  divides this sum and we're done because  $p \mid n$ . If  $j = k$  then this sum is exactly equal to  $p$  and we're done as well.

It remains to prove the result when  $n$  is squarefree. We proceed by induction on the number of prime factors of  $n$ . If  $n$  is prime then all of the prime factors of  $\phi(n) = n - 1$  must divide  $n$ , which implies  $n - 1 = 1$  because no prime less than  $n$  divides  $n$ . The result is now evident. Now assume  $n = p_1p_2 \cdots p_r$  for some  $r \geq 2$ , where  $p_1 < p_2 < \cdots < p_r$  are prime. Let  $n^{*} = p_1p_2\cdots p_{r - 1}$ . We now prove that  $v_{p_i}(\Sigma(n, k)) \geq v_{p_i}(\phi(n^{*})) + v_{p_i}(p_r - 1) = v_{p_i}(\phi(n))$  for  $i = 1, 2, \dots, r - 1$ . We begin by proving the following lemma:**Lemma.** For any two integers  $n, k$  with  $n$  positive and  $k$  non-negative and any prime  $p$  we have  $v_p(1^k + 2^k + \dots + n^k) \geq v_p(n) - 1$ .

*Proof.* It suffices to prove the result for primes dividing  $n$ . Let  $p^a$  be the maximal power of  $p$  dividing  $n$ . By taking mod  $p^a$  we see that it suffices to prove that  $p^{a - 1}$  divides  $1^k + 2^k + \dots + (p^a)^k$ . We proceed by induction on  $a$ . The base case  $a = 1$  is trivial. Now by the Binomial Theorem we have  $(i + mp^a)^k \equiv i^k \pmod{p^a}$ , and thus  $$ \sum_{i = 1}^{p^{a + 1}} i^k = \sum_{i = 1}^{p^a}\sum_{j = 0}^{p - 1} (i + jp^a)^k \equiv \sum_{i = 1}^{p^a}\sum_{j = 0}^{p - 1} i^k = p\left(\sum_{i = 1}^{p^a} i^k\right) \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{a}} $$  Because  $p^{a - 1}$  divides this sum by the induction hypothesis. This proves the lemma.

Now consider the sum  $\sum_{s \in S_{n^{*}}}\sum_{i = 0}^{p_r - 1} (s + in^{*})^k$ . This is equal to  $\Sigma(n, k)$ , except for the terms that are divisible by  $p_r$  and no other of our primes, which we'll deal with later. However, we first manipulate this previous sum as follows:  $$ \sum_{s \in S_{n^{*}}}\sum_{i = 0}^{p_r - 1} (s + in^{*})^k = \sum_{s \in S_{n^{*}}}\sum_{i = 0}^{p_r - 1}\sum_{j = 0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}s^j(in^{*})^{k - j} = \sum_{j = 0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}\left(\sum_{i = 0}^{p_r - 1} (in^{*})^{k - j}\right)\left(\sum_{s \in S_{n^{*}}} s^j\right) = \sum_{j = 0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}\left(n^{*}\right)^{k - j}\left(\sum_{i = 0}^{p_r - 1}i^{k - j}\right)\Sigma(S_{n^{*}}, j) $$  By our lemma we have  $v_{p_i}\left(\sum_{i = 0}^{p_r - 1} i^{k - j}\right) \geq v_{p_i}(p_r - 1) - 1$  for  $0 \leq j \leq k - 1$ . Because  $v_{p_i}(n^{*}) \geq 1$  it follows that  $$ v_{p_i}\left(\binom{k}{j}\left(n^{*}\right)^{k - j}\left(\sum_{i = 0}^{p_r - 1}i^{k - j}\right)\Sigma(S_{n^{*}}, j)\right) \geq v_{p_i}(\Sigma(S_{n^{*}}, j)) + v_{p_i}(p_r - 1) $$  And because  $v_{p_i}(\Sigma(S_{n^{*}})) \geq v_{p_i}(\phi(n^{*}))$  by induction hypothesis, all of these terms vanish modulo  $p_i^{v_{p_i}(\phi(n))}$ . We are left with  $p_r(\Sigma(S_{n^{*}}, k))$ . Now, the terms divisible by  $p_r$  which we previously neglected are those of the form  $(p_rs)^k$  where  $s \in S_{n^{*}}$  (because no  $p_i$  other than  $p_r$  may divide them), and thus their sum is equal to  $p_r^k(\Sigma(S_{n^{*}}, k))$ . Finally this implies that modulo  $p_i^{v_{p_i}(\phi(n))}$ :  $$ \Sigma(S_n, k) \equiv (p_r - p_r^k)\Sigma(S_{n^{*}}, k) = -p_r(p_r^{k - 1} - 1)\Sigma(S_{n^{*}}, k) $$  Because  $p_r - 1 \mid p_r^{k - 1} - 1$  it follows that  $v_{p_i}(\Sigma(S_n, k)) \geq v_{p_i}(p_r - 1) + v_{p_i}(\Sigma(S_{n^{*}}, k)) \geq v_{p_i}(p_r - 1) + v_{p_i}(\phi(n^{*})) = v_{p_i}(\phi(n))$ , as desired. Because every prime factor of  $\phi(n)$  is a prime factor of  $n$ , and  $p_r$  does not divide  $\phi(n) = (p_1 - 1)(p_2 - 1)\cdots(p_r - 1)$ , we are done.

We will show that for any prime  $p$ , if  $v_p(m)=M$ , then  $p^M\mid a_1^k+a_2^k+\cdots+a_m^k$  for all  $k\ge0$ . The problem then clearly follows from this. Call a set  $S$  of integers  $p^M$ -happy if  $p^M\mid\sum_{a\in S}a^k$  for all  $k\ge0$ .

The first key observation is that if  $S$  is  $p^M$ -happy, then  $S+i=\{a+i\mid a\in S\}$  is  $p^M$ -happy for any integer  $i$ . Indeed, we have that  $\sum_{a\in S}(a+i)^k=\sum_{j=0}^k\left(\binom kji^{k-j}\sum_{a\in S}a^j\right)$  is divisible by  $p^M$  as  $p^M\mid\sum_{a\in S}a^j$  for all  $j$ .

The second key observation is that if  $S$  is  $p^M$ -happy, then  $S_{i,M,c}=\{a+bip^M\mid a\in S, 1\le b\le p^c\}$  is  $p^{M+c}$ -happy for any integer  $i$  and positive integer  $c$ . For  $c=1$ , this is clearly true for  $k=0$  as  $|S_i|=p|S|$ . For  $k>0$  we have that  $\sum_{a\in S}\sum_{b=1}^p(a+bip^M)^k\equiv p\sum_{a\in S}a^k+\frac{p(p+1)}2\cdot kip^M\sum_{a\in S}a^{k-1}\pmod{p^{M+1}}$  by the Binomial Theorem, as the  $p^{jM}$  terms vanish mod  $p^{M+1}$  for  $j>1$ . This then clearly vanishes mod  $p^{M+1}$  as  $p^M\mid\sum_{a\in S}a^k,\sum_{a\in S}a^{k-1}$ , as desired. For  $c>1$ , note that  $S_{i,M,c}=T_{i,M+1,c-1}$ , where  $T=S_{i,M,1}$  is  $p^{M+1}$ -happy, so the observation follows by induction on  $c$ .

Let  $n=p^ep_1^{e_1}p_2^{e_2}\cdots p_r^{e_r}$  be the prime factorization of  $n$ . We claim that it suffices to prove the result in the case of  $e_1=e_2=\cdots=e_r=1$ . Indeed, if  $n'=p^ep_1p_2\cdots p_r$ , then  $v_p(\varphi(n'))=M$ . Furthermore, if  $A$  is the set of positive integers less than  $n'$  that are relatively prime to  $n$ , then the set of positive integers less than  $n$  that are relatively prime to  $n$  is  $A\cup A+n'\cup A+2n'\cup\cdots\cup A+n-n'$ . The first key observation tells us that  $A,A+n',A+2n',\ldots,A+n-n'$  are all  $p^M$ -happy, so their disjoint union is as well, as desired.

Say a prime  $q$  is sad if  $p\mid q-1$ . We now induct on the number of sad prime factors of  $n$ . For the base case of  $n$  having no sad prime factors, we have that  $v_p(n)=M+1$ . This is done by the Chinese Remainder Theorem; we simply partition the integers by their residue modulo  $\frac n{p^{M+1}}$ . This proof is divided into two parts. The first is reducing the problem to squarefree  $n$ , and the second is solving it for squarefree  $n$ .
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------**Reducing to Squarfree**
Let  $\Phi(n)$  be the set of numbers less than or equal to  $n$  that are relatively prime to  $n$ . Note that  $\varphi(n)=|\Phi(n)|$ . We will need an important lemma.

<u>Lemma 1:</u> If  $r\mid x$ , then  $\Phi(xr)=\Phi(x)\cup(\Phi(x)+x)\cup(\Phi(x)+2x)\cup\cdots\cup(\Phi(x)+(r-1)x)$ .

<u>Proof of Lemma 1:</u> The main point here is that  $\gcd(y,xr)=1$  if and only if  $\gcd(y,x)=1$ . The left hand side is simply those numbers that are relatively prime to  $x$  and are at most  $rx$ .  $\blacksquare$ Here is the main claim.

<u>**Claim 1:**</u> If  $p\mid n'$  and the problem holds for  $n'$ , then it also holds for  $n=pn'$ .

<u>Proof of Claim 1:</u> Let  $m'=\varphi(n')$ , and let  $m=\varphi(n)=pm'$ . We want to show that  $m$  divides
\[S:=\sum_{a\in\Phi(n)}a^k.\]
By lemma 1, we can rewrite this as
\[S = \sum_{a\in\Phi(n')}\sum_{\ell=0}^{p-1}(a+n'\ell)^k.\]
We now see that
\begin{align*}
S &= \sum_{a\in\Phi(n')}\sum_{\ell=0}^{p-1}\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{k}{j}a^{k-j}(n'\ell)^j 
&= \sum_{j=0}^k\binom{k}{j}\left(\sum_{\ell=0}^{p-1}(n'\ell)^j\sum_{a\in\Phi(n')}a^{k-j}\right)
\end{align*}
Note that  $\sum_{a\in\Phi(n')}a^{k-j}$  is a multiple of  $m'=m/p$  by the premise of the claim. For  $j=0$ , the summand looks like  $p\sum_{a\in\Phi(n')}a^{k-j}$ , which is then a multiple of  $p$ , and for  $j\ge 1$ , we see that  $p\mid(n'\ell)^j$  (we had  $p\mid n'$ ), so the terms are all divisible by  $m$  anyway. Therefore, we see that  $m\mid S$ , as desired.  $\blacksquare$ If the problem is true for  $n=p_1\cdots p_k$ , then by the claim, it is true for  $n=p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_k^{e_k}$  for all  $e_1,\ldots,e_k\ge 1$  (essentially by induction), so this part of the overall proof is complete.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------**Solving for Squarefree**
This part is significantly harder than the previous part, and it will also employ the condition that all primes that divide  $\varphi(n)$  divide  $n$ . Suppose the problem is true for  $n'=p_1\cdots p_r$ . Now suppose  $n=n'p$  where we have that  $\varphi(p)=p-1=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_r^{a_r}$  for some  $a_1,\cdots a_r\ge 0$ , and not all are  $0$ . We show that the problem is true for  $n$  as well.

We are going to need a somewhat ad-hoc lemma for this.

<u>Lemma 2:</u> Let  $S_k(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{x}j^k$ . Viewing  $S_k(x)$  as a polynomial in  $x$ , we can write it as  $\frac{x}{(k+1)!}$  times an integer polynomial.

<u>Proof of Lemma 2:</u> We proceed by induction on  $k$ .  $k=0$  is obvious, so assume its true for all  $k'<k$ . Note that
\[x^{k+1}=\sum_{j=1}^{x}(j^{k+1}-(j-1)^{k+1})=\sum_{j=1}^{x}\sum_{\ell=0}^{k}\binom{k+1}{\ell}j^\ell(-1)^{k+1-\ell}.\]
Therefore, there are integers  $c_\ell$  such that
\[x^{k+1}=\sum_{\ell=0}^k c_\ell S_\ell(x).\]
In particular,  $c_k=\pm(k+1)$ . We note that
\[\sum_{\ell=0}^{k-1}c_\ell S_\ell(x)\]
is divisible by  $x$  and can be written as an integer polynomial over  $\mathrm{lcm}(1!,2!,\ldots,k!)=k!$  by the inductive hypothesis. Therefore,
\[(k+1)S_k(x) = \pm x^{k+1}+\frac{xp(x)}{k!}\]
for some integer polynomial  $p(x)$ . Dividing by  $k+1$ , the result follows by induction.  $\blacksquare$ We first need a modification of lemma 1. Here, we see that
\[\Phi(n) = \left(\Phi(n')\cup(\Phi(n')+n')\cup\cdots\cup(\Phi(n')+(p-1)n')\right)\setminus\{p\Phi(n')\cup p^2\Phi(n')\cup p^3\Phi(n')\cdots\}.\]
However, we have that  $p\Phi(n')\subset\Phi(n')$  since  $\gcd(p,n')=1$ , so in fact
\[p\Phi(n')\supset p^2\Phi(n')\supset p^3\Phi(n')\supset\cdots.\]
Therefore, we just have
\[\Phi(n) = \left(\Phi(n')\cup(\Phi(n')+n')\cup\cdots\cup(\Phi(n')+(p-1)n')\right)\setminus\{p\Phi(n')\}.\]
Thus,
\[S:=\sum_{a\in\Phi(n)}a^k = \sum_{a\in\Phi(n')}\sum_{\ell=0}^{p-1}(a+n'\ell)^k-p^k\sum_{a\in\Phi(n')}a^k.\]
As in the previous part, we can reduce this to
\[S=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom{k}{j}\left(\sum_{\ell=0}^{p-1}(n'\ell)^j\sum_{a\in\Phi(n')}a^{k-j}\right)-p^k\sum_{a\in\Phi(n')}a^k.\]
Note that this can be viewed is a linear combination of the  $x_g:=\sum_{a\in\Phi(n')}a^g$  where  $g\ge 0$ , and since each of these are divisibly by  $\varphi(n')$ , it suffices to show that each of their coefficients is divisible by  $\varphi(n)/\varphi(n')=\varphi(p)=p-1$ . Note that the coefficient of  $x_0$  is  $p-p^k$ , which is clearly divisble by  $p-1$ , as desired.

We now look at the coefficient of  $x_{k-g}$  where  $g\ge k-1$ . We see that it is
\[c_g = \binom{k}{g}(n')^g\sum_{\ell=0}^{p-1}\ell^g.\]
By lemma 2,  $c_g/(p-1)$  is then some integer times  $(n')^g/(g+1)!$ . Now  $\nu_{p_i}((n')^g)=g$ , and  $\nu_{p_i}((g+1)!)<\frac{g+1}{p_i-1}\le g+1$  by Legendre's theorem. Therefore,  $\nu_{p_i}((n')^g/(g+1)!)\ge 0$ . Therefore,  $\nu_{p_i}(c_g/(p-1))\ge 0$  for all  $1\le i\le r$ .

Here is where the problem's premise comes in. Note that all of the prime factors of  $p-1$  are of the form  $p_i$ , so if  $\nu_{p_i}(c_g/(p-1))\ge 0$  for all  $p_i$ , then in fact  $c_g/(p-1)$  is an integer.

Thus,  $\varphi(p)=p-1\mid c_g$  for all  $0\le g\le k$ , and we have  $\varphi(n')\mid x_g$  for all  $0\le g\le k$ . Thus,
\[\varphi(n)=\varphi(p)\varphi(n')\mid S=c_0x_0+\cdots+c_kx_k.\]

Therefore, we have gotten from  $p_1\cdots p_r$  to  $p_1\cdots p_rp$ . The case of  $r=0$  is trivially satisfied, so by induction, we have solved the problem for all squarefree  $n$ .

We will use induction. That is, if we can prove the case  $n$ , then we can prove the case  $pn$  ,  $(p \in P)$ . Of course, we need the condition that  $\operatorname{rad} \varphi(np) \mid np$ . Considering two cases: $\textcolor{red}{\text{Case 1.}}$   $p \mid n.$  Then
\[
\{a \in \mathbb{N}^*,\, a < n,\, (a, pn) = 1\} = \{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{\varphi(n)}, n+a_1, \ldots, n+a_{\varphi(n)}, \ldots, (p-1)n + a_1, \ldots, (p-1)n + a_{\varphi(n)}\}.
\]
Let  $S_k = a_1^k + a_2^k + \ldots + a_{\varphi(n)}^k.$  Then, we need to prove that
\[
p \varphi(n) \mid \sum_{i=1}^{\varphi(n)} (a_i^k + (n+a_i)^k + \ldots + ((p-1)n + a_i)^k)
\]
which is equivalent to
\[
p \varphi(n) \mid p S_k + \sum_{j=1}^{k} \binom{k}{j} n^j \left( \sum_{t=1}^{p-1} t^j \right) S_{k-j},
\]
which is true by the induction hypothesis. $\textcolor{red}{\text{Case 2.}}$   $p \nmid n.$  Then
\[
\{a \in \mathbb{N}^*,\, a < n,\, (a, pn) = 1\} = \{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{\varphi(n)}, n+a_1, \ldots, n+a_{\varphi(n)}, \ldots, (p-1)n + a_1, \ldots, (p-1)n + a_{\varphi(n)}\} \setminus \{p a_1, p a_2, \ldots, p a_{\varphi(n)}\}.
\]
So, we need to prove that
\[
(p-1)\varphi(n) \mid p S_k + \sum_{j=1}^{k} \binom{k}{j} n^j \left( \sum_{t=1}^{p-1} t^j \right) S_{k-j} - p^k S_k.
\]
Since  $(p-1)\varphi(n) \mid p S_k - p^k S_k$ , the above formula is equivalent to
\[
(p-1)\varphi(n) \mid \sum_{j=1}^{k} \binom{k}{j} n^j \left( \sum_{t=1}^{p-1} t^j \right) S_{k-j}.
\]
Now, we only need to prove that
\[
p-1 \mid n \sum_{t=1}^{p-1} t^j.
\]
Now, we continue with some lemmas. $\textcolor{red}{\text{Lemma 1.}}$  Given a prime  $q$ , and positive integers  $j, s$ , then
\[
s - 1 \le \nu_q(1^j + 2^j + \ldots + (q^s - 1)^j).
\] $\textcolor{red}{\text{Proof.}}$ First, consider that  $q$  is odd. Let  $g$  be a primitive root modulo  $q^s$ . Then
\[
1^j + 2^j + \ldots + (q^s - 1)^j = \sum_{k=0}^{\varphi(q^s)-1} g^{jk} + \sum_{l=1}^{q^{s-1}} (lq)^{j} = \dfrac{(g^j)^{\varphi(q^s)} - 1}{g^j - 1} + \ldots,
\]
and we are done by LTE.

Now consider that  $q = 2$ . We don't have a primitive root modulo  $2^s$  ( $s \ge 3$ ), but we can still use  $5$ . Then

\{1, 5^1, 5^2, 5^3, \ldots, 5^{\varphi(2^s)/2 - 1}\}
\]
will cover exactly half of the odd members in  $\mathbb{Z}/2^s\mathbb{Z}$ . Then we use the same method as in the case  $q$  is odd. $\textcolor{red}{\text{Lemma 2.}}$  Given a prime  $q$ , and positive integers  $k, l$ . Then
\[
\nu_q(1^k + 2^k + \ldots + l^k) \ge \nu_q(l) - 1.
\]
This follows immediately from Lemma 1, and also completes the remaining part of the proof.

stem_md:
Let  $a_n$  be the number of permutations  $(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n)$  of the numbers  $(1,2,\dots, n)$  such that the  $n$  ratios  $\frac{x_k}{k}$  for  $1\le k\le n$  are all distinct. Prove that  $a_n$  is odd for all  $n\ge 1$ .

*Proposed by Richard Stong*
solution_md:
My solution was 14 pages long. I've discussed this problem with a bunch of other moppers, and I'm pretty sure I'm the only one who actually solved the problem, due to a common mistake that most of the MOPpers made. Props to a1267ab for also finding a correct solution, and thank you to qbzvavba for helping to demonstrate just how hard this problem really is.

EDIT: I've been made aware that a1267ab is a MOPper. Evidently, I'm not the only MOPper who solved it. 

<details><summary>Solution (finished)</summary>Where to begin? (motivation part 1):

There are three motivational ideas that most people who made progress on this problem came up with. 

The first is that if  $\sigma$  is a permutation which satisfies the conditions of the problem, then so is  $\sigma^{-1}$ . This is because the ratios of  $\sigma^{-1}$  are exactly the reciprocals of the permutations of  $\sigma$ , so if any two of the  $\sigma$  ratios are the same, then so are two of the  $\sigma^{-1}$  ratios, and vice versa. This means that we only need to deal with those permutations which are *involutions*: permutations which are their own inverse. We can further restrict what kinds of involutions are allowed: a permutation which satisfies the conditions of the problem can only have the ratio  $1$  appear at most once, so the involutions can have at most one fixed point. 

The second is that it is very easy to find the number of involutions with at most one fixed point. As you'll see later in the proof, this number is always odd.

Putting these two facts together, the problem opens itself up to a new approach: complementary counting. If we can show that the number of involutions with at most one fixed point that DON'T satisfy the problem conditions is even, then we are done. This seems like a possibility due to the third (and most important) motivating idea, which I'll call "the fraction swap." The idea is that if  $\sigma(a)=b$  and  $\sigma(c)=d$ , with  $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}$ , then you can swap  $b$  and  $c$  to get  $\sigma'$  ( $\sigma'(a)=c$ , $\sigma'(b)=d$ ) which also doesn't satisfy the problem conditions. Unfortunately, using this alone to try to prove that there are an even number of bad permutations has problems, which I'll highlight in the actual meat of the proof.
-----
Proof part 1:

Let's start with some definitions. Let  $A$  be the set of permutations on  $n$  elements which satisfy the problem statement, and let  $B$  be the set of involutions on  $n$  elements with at most one fixed point. From the explanation in the first paragraph of my "motivation part 1" section, we know that  $|A - B|$  is even.

To count the size of  $B$ , first consider what such involutions must look like. If  $n$  is even, there can be no fixed points, because since the non-fixed points are each cycles of length 2, parity tells us that there must be at least two fixed points, a contradiction. Similarly, if  $n$  is odd, there must be exactly one fixed point. Thus we can count the size of  $B$ : When  $n$  is even, it's the number of way to partition  $n$  things into  $\frac{n}{2}$  unordered pairs, which is just  $\frac{n!}{2^{n/2}*\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)!} = (n-1)(n-3)(\cdots)(1)$ , which is clearly odd. Similarly, when  $n$  is odd, after a small variation thanks to the fixed point we get  $|B|=n(n-2)(\cdots)(1)$ , which is also clearly odd. Thus,  $|B|$  is odd.

The final step is to show that  $|B - A|$  is even. So this is where we use the fraction swap and win... right?
-----
The Trap (motivation part 2):

Many, many, MANY people tried to move forward from here using the "fraction swap" trick I mentioned. Unfortunately, it just doesn't work. qbzvavba's wrong solution shows the direction that most people tried to take it. Some MOPpers tried to be a bit more sophisticated about it and be more specific to get around the issues involved. A common trick they tried was to specifically do the fraction swap on the "smallest" pair of pairs, by some metric of "smallest," but this trick certainly doesn't work (the example of  $(12)(34)(68)(57)$  should explain why. 

After working on the problem for a while, and actually solving it for myself, I can say that I'm 99% sure that **THERE IS NO NICE INVOLUTION ON THE BAD PERMUTATIONS IN  $B$**. 

That doesn't mean the fraction swap is completely useless, however. We can still use it for motivation. While the fraction swap doesn't kill the problem like we may have wanted it to, it DOES give us the idea that we can "move between" various permutations. It also gives us the idea that we should be able to "pair up" things in a certain way. Basically, the fraction swap motivates us to continue trying the complementary counting technique.

The way that I and a few others moved forward from here was using PIE. Basically, fraction swap DOES tell us one useful thing: by a certain metric, the number of ways that a permutation can "be bad" is even. That metric motivates the introduction of the set  $P$ , using it to divide  $B-A$  into subsets, and then using PIE. ( $P$  also completely ruins me trying to explain my solution out loud to anyone due to the confusingness of "pairs of pairs.")
---
Proof part 2:

Let  $P$  be the set of all pairs  $\{\{(a,b),(c,d)\}|a,b,c,d \le n, \mathrm{all\ distinct}, ad=bc, a<b\}$ . That last condition could probably be removed, but it makes the rest of the proof a tad easier.

Given a set of pairs  $\{(a_1,b_1),(a_2,b_2),\cdots,(a_k,b_k)|a_i,b_i \le n \mathrm{\ for\  all\ } 1 \le i \le k\}$ , we call the set "consistent" if all of the  $a_i,b_i$  are distinct (i.e. there are  $2k$  distinct values). 

These two definitions might seem weird, but they're both consequences of the same concept: we're going to use sets of pairs to represent forced parts of involutions.  $P$  is defined such that if  $\{(a,b),(c,d)\} \in P$ , any  $\sigma \in B$  which has both  $\sigma(a)=b$  and  $\sigma(c)=d$  must not be in  $A$  (in cycle notation,  $\sigma$  would have (a,b) and (c,d) in it, which makes these pairs of pairs make even more sense). "Consistency" is just the idea that we shouldn't force any one element to map to two different things in the involution.

Now, given a consistent set  $S=\{(a_1,b_1),\cdots,(a_k,b_k)\}$ , define  $B_{S}$  to be the set of involutions  $\sigma \in B$  such that  $\sigma(a_1)=b_1,\cdots,\sigma(a_k)=b_k$ . Note that  $|B_{S}|$  is odd; we can see this because  $|B_{S}|$  is just the number of involutions of the  $n-2k$  unused elements with at most one fixed point; as we know from part 1, the number of involutions of a set with at most one fixed point is always odd. 

From here, note that every involution in  $B-A$  ("bad" involution) must be in  $B_p$  for some  $p \in P$ , so  $\cup_{p \in P} B_p = B-A$ . Thus, by PIE,
\begin{align*}
|B-A|&=\sum_{X \subseteq P} \left|\cap_{p \in X} B_p\right| 
 &= \sum_{X \subseteq P, \cup_{p \in X} p \mathrm{\ consistent}} |B_{\cup_{p \in X} p}| 
 &\equiv |\{X \subseteq P, \cup_{p \in X} p \mathrm{\ consistent}\}| \pmod{2}
\end{align*}

We now want to prove that  $|\{X \subseteq P, \cup_{p \in X} p \mathrm{\ consistent}\}|$  is even.
---
THUNK (motivation part 3):

So at this point, we've rephrased the problem. We need to show that the number of consistent sets of illegal pairs of pairs is even. The problem is... that's a WEIRD thing to think about.

If you consider the concept for a bit, you'll understand why it's so weird. While it's easy to think about sets of pairs (they're restrictions on what the involution can be), it's EXTREMELY unusual to think about sets of pairs of pairs -- especially when it's not always "closed upward" in some fashion (e.g. when  $n=8$ , one of the sets  $X$  is  $\{\{(1,2),(3,6)\},\{(1,2),(4,8)\}\}$ , which is unusual because it doesn't have  $\{(3,6),(4,8)\}$ , even though that's technically also a restriction).

I spent probably the majority of the contest thinking about this. (I was thinking about calling this section "thinking way too f***ing hard"). In the end, the breakthrough idea was to group together all of the sets of pairs that represented the same restriction. This led to the definition of "similar" sets (sets which represent the same restriction) and "similarity classes."

However, another important thing to think about is the idea that sets of illegal pairs of pairs can be broken up into parts based on which common ratio each pair of pairs has. For example, if my set of pairs is  $\{\{(1,2),(3,6)\},\{(4,8),(7,14)\},\{(5,11),(10,22)\}\}$ , I should think about (1,2),(3,6) and (4,8),(7,14) together, since they share a ratio, and thus any pair of those four pairs will be an illegal pair. However, (5,11),(10,22) share a different common ratio, so they won't ever go together with (1,2),(3,6),(4,8), or (7,14). The idea that things with the same ratio go together, while things with different ratios don't, goes into the idea of the "ratio subclass," and is the motivation for the upcoming Ratio Subclass Lemma. 
---
Proof part 3:

Two sets  $X_1,X_2 \subseteq P$  are said to be *similar* if  $\cup_{p \in X_1} p = \cup_{p \in X_2} p$ ; these sets are said to be in the "similarity class" of the set  $\cup_{p \in X_1} p$  (this set is NOT the class itself, just a label for the class). Note that similarity is a congruence relation, so the similarity classes partition  $\{X \subseteq P | \cup_{p \in X} p \mathrm{\ consistent}\}$ . If we can get a sense of the sizes of the similarity classes, we can get closer to figuring out the parity of the whole set, which is what we want.

Given a similarity class set  $C$  and a rational number  $r$ , the *ratio subclass*  $C_r \subseteq C$  is the set  $\{(a,b) \in C | \frac{a}{b}=r\}$ . That is, it's the set of pairs in  $C$  with a given ratio.

This next lemma is hard to motivate unless you've played around with the problem a lot, but it comes pretty naturally from trying to figure out stuff about the similarity classes using ratio subclasses. That's why it's called the Ratio Subclass Lemma.**The Ratio Subclass Lemma:** For a nonnegative integer  $x$ , let  $f(x)$  be the number of families of two-element subsets of a set  $S$  of size  $x$  such that the union of the two-element subsets is all of  $S$ . Then  $f(x)$  is even iff  $x$  is odd. 

*Proof*: We proceed by induction on  $x$ . For simplicity, I'll do two base cases: $x=0$ :  $f(0)$  is clearly 1 -- the empty family. $x=1$ :  $f(1)$  is clearly 0 -- either the family is empty (and thus the union is empty), or it contains a two-element subset (so its union has at least two elements).

For the inductive step, suppose the statements holds for all  $x<k$  for some positive integer  $k \ge 2$ . Now, consider a set  $S$  of size  $k$ . Note that any family of two-element subsets of  $S$  will have a union which is a subset of  $S$ . Note also that if  $T$  is a subset of  $S$ , the number of such families which have a union equal to  $T$  is clearly exactly  $f(|T|)$ , since those families are exactly the ones where all of the subsets are subsets of  $T$  and have union equal to  $T$ . We thus have
\begin{align*}
2^{\binom{k}{2}}&=\sum_{T \subseteq S} f(|T|)=\sum_{i=0}^{k} \binom{k}{i} f(i) 
&\equiv f(k)+\sum_{i=0}^{\left\lfloor\frac{k-1}{2}\right\rfloor} \binom{k}{2i} \pmod{2}
\end{align*}

It is well-known that  $\sum_{i=0}^{\left\lfloor\frac{k}{2}\right\rfloor} \binom{k}{2i} = 2^{k-1}$ . When  $k$  is even,  $\sum_{i=0}^{\left\lfloor\frac{k-1}{2}\right\rfloor} \binom{k}{2i}$  is missing the last term  $\binom{k}{k}$ , so the sum is  $2^{k-1}-1 \equiv 1 \pmod{2}$ ; when  $k$  is odd, there is no missing last term, so the sum is  $2^{k-1} \equiv 0 \pmod{2}$ . Since  $2^{\binom{k}{2}} \equiv 0 \pmod{2}$ , we see that  $f(k) \equiv 1 \pmod{2}$  when  $k$  is even, and  $f(k) \equiv 0 \pmod{2}$  when  $k$  is odd, as desired.  $\blacksquare$ Now, for a set of pairs of pairs  $X$  to be in a given similarity class  $C$ , one can see that there are exactly two conditions: (a)  $X$  must contain all of the pairs in  $C$  in at least one of its pairs, and no other pairs; and (b) every pair of pairs in  $X$  must have both pairs come from the same ratio subclass of  $C$ . In particular, for each non-empty ratio subclass  $C_r$  of  $C$ ,  $X$  must have a subset  $X_r$  which "covers"  $C_r$  and only  $C_r$ . This partitions  $X$  into disjoint subsets, each of which is a set of two-element subsets of some  $C_r$  whose union is all of  $C_r$ . This looks just like the Ratio Subclass Lemma! Applying the lemma tells us that the number of possible choices for  $X$  is  $\prod_{r \in \mathbb R, C_r \neq \emptyset} f(|C_r|)$ . When one of the  $C_r$  has odd size, the similarity class has even size, by the lemma. Otherwise, when all of the  $C_r$  have even size, the similarity class has odd size. 

We now just need to prove that there are an odd number of similarity classes with ratio subclasses of all even size. We'll call a similarity class with ratio subclasses of all even size an ESSC (Even Subclass Similarity Class).
---
It all comes together (motivation part 4):

This is it. The last step. The one that comes out of nowhere.

If you've been paying attention, you might have noticed that I haven't actually used the "fraction swap" yet. Sure, it motivated me to look at PIE, but I never ended up using it there. It seems incredible to think that one could solve this problem without using it even once. 

After poking around a lot with the fraction swap at the start of the problem, I noticed that it split up the bad involutions in a graph-like way. Involutions were "connected" if they were one fraction swap away. If I were REALLY smart (like a1267ab), I would have played around more with this idea and solved the problem in a much more reasonable fashion. Yet, here I was, 11 pages deep and going nowhere fast. I had this strange looking ratio subclass condition -- how could I use that?

The entire time I was thinking about part 3, I was thinking about ways that I could relate two similarity classes using the fraction swap, but I was having trouble because the fraction swap messed with the ratio subclasses. Once I got to this point, I realized that the fraction swap paired similarity classes with all even ratio subclasses to each other... but not in an involution-like way. More... in a graph-like way.

I knew one way to use graphs to prove something is even: if a graph has all vertices of odd degree, it has an even number of vertices. With this in the back of my mind, thinking about connecting various similarity classes using the fraction swap, I eventually came up with the trick, and the final step of my proof.

(Fun fact: on my solution paper, I have two lines dedicated just to the words "How? GRAPH THEORY.")
---
Proof part 4:

Given a similarity class  $C$ , let  $N(C)$  be the set of numbers that are in at least one of the pairs in  $C$  (e.g. if  $C=\{(1,2),(3,6),(4,8)\}$ , then  $V=\{1,2,3,4,6,8\}$ ). For each distinct possible  $N(C)$  (with  $C$  an ESSC), define a graph  $G=(V,E)$ , where  $V$  is the set of all ESSCs with the given  $N(C)$ , and  $C_1,C_2 \in V$  are adjacent if there are some  $(a,b),(c,d) \in C_1$  with  $a=\min(N(C))$  and  $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}$  such that  $C_2=(C_1 - \{(a,b),(c,d)\}) \cup \{(a,c),(b,d)\}$ . Note that this process removes two pairs from one ratio subclass and adds two pairs to another ratio subclass, so every possible  $(a,b),(c,d) \in C_1$  which satisfies the conditions will correspond to an edge of the graph.

Note that we're finally using the fraction swap! Classes are adjacent if they're one fraction swap away from each other. However, I'm being very careful here: fraction swaps are only allowed if they involve the smallest element of  $N(C)$ . Since  $N(C)$  is fixed for all of the classes involved, this is OK.

Lastly, note that since  $\min(N(C))$  is in exactly one pair for each class, and since there are an even number of total pairs in its ratio subclass, there are one less than an even number of edges for each class -- in other words, every class has an odd number of edges. Since graphs with all vertices of odd degree must have an even number of vertices, there is are an even number of ESSCs for each valid  $N(C)$ , and in particular an even number of ESSCs total. This completes the proof -- in full.</details>

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>This is the official solution; the proof has two main insights.

The first idea:**Lemma**:  	If a permutation  $x$  works, 	so does the inverse permutation.

Thus it suffices to consider permutations  $x$  in which all cycles have length at most  $2$ . Of course, there can be at most one fixed point (since that gives the ratio  $1$ ), and hence exactly one if  $n$  is odd, none if  $n$  is even.

We consider the graph  $K_n$  such that the edge  $\{i,j\}$  is labeled with  $i / j$  (for  $i < j$ ). The permutations we're considering are then equivalent to maximal matchings of this  $K_n$ . We call such a matching *fantastic* if it has an all of distinct edge labels.

\bigskip

Now the second insight is that if edges  $ab$  and  $cd$  have the same label for  $a<b$  and  $c<d$ , then so do edges  $ac$  and  $bd$ . Thus:**Definition**:  	Given a matching  $\mathcal M$  as above we say the *neighbors* 	of  $\mathcal M$  are those other matchings obtained as follows: 	for each label  $\ell$ , 	we take some pairs of edges (possibly none) 	with label  $\ell$  and apply the above switching operation.

The second observation is that:**Claim**:  	The matching  $\mathcal M$  has an even number of neighbors 	(including itself) if and only if it is not fantastic.

*Proof.*  	Consider the label  $\ell$ , 	and assume it appears  $n_\ell \ge 1$  times.

If we pick  $k$  disjoint pairs and swap them, 	the number of ways to do this is 	 $\binom{n_\ell}{2k} (2k-1)!!$ , and so the total 	number of ways to perform operations on the edges 	labeled  $\ell$  is 	\[ \sum_k \binom{n_\ell}{2k} (2k-1)!! 		\equiv \sum_k \binom{n_\ell}{2k} 		= 2^{n_\ell-1} \pmod 2. 	\] 	This is even if and only if  $n_\ell > 1$ .

Finally, note that the number of neighbors 	of  $\mathcal M$  is the product across all  $\ell$  of the above. 	So it is odd if and only if each factor is odd, 	if and only if  $n_\ell = 1$  for every  $\ell$ .  $\blacksquare$ To finish, consider a huge simple graph  $\Gamma$  on all the maximal matchings, with edge relations given by neighbor relation. Observe that:  	
- Fantastic matchings correspond to isolated vertices 	(of degree zero, with no other neighbors) of  $\Gamma$ .
- The rest of the vertices of  $\Gamma$  have odd degrees 	(one less than the neighbor count)
- The graph  $\Gamma$  has an even number of vertices of odd degree 	(this is true for any simple graph, see ``handshake lemma'').
- The number of vertices of  $\Gamma$  is odd, 	namely  $\left( 2\left\lceil n/2 \right\rceil - 1 \right)!!$ .
 This concludes the proof.</details>

The case  $n=1$  is obvious. Suppose  $n>1$ .

We call a permutation bad if  $\frac{x_k}{k}$  are not all distinct and good otherwise. Now notice that if  $\sigma$  is good then so is  $\sigma^{-1}$ . Therefore, if  $\sigma$  is good and  $\sigma^2\neq I$  then we can pair it up with another permutation  $\sigma^{-1}$ .

Therefore, define  $$ S=\{\sigma(\sigma(x))=x\forall x:\sigma\in S_n\} $$  It suffices to show that the number of good permutations in this set is odd. Indeed every permutation in  $S$  can always be decomposed into  $2$ -cycles and fixed points, and every good permutation contains at most  $1$  fixed points. Therefore, good permutation in  $S$  consists of  $1$  fixed points and  $\frac{n-1}{2}$   $2$ -cycles if  $n$  is odd and  $\frac{n}{2}$   $2$ -cycles if  $n$  is even.

Define  $T$  to be the set of permutations with  $1$  fixed points and  $\frac{n-1}{2}$   $2$ -cycles if  $n$  is odd and the set of permutations with  $\frac{n}{2}$   $2$ -cycles if  $n$  is even.

Notice that by simple counting we obtain  $$ |T|=\begin{cases}1\cdot 3\cdot...\cdot(n-2)\cdot n&\text{if  $n$  is odd}
1\cdot3\cdot...\cdot(n-1)&\text{if  $n$  is even}\end{cases} $$  which is odd in odd cases. Therefore, it suffices to show that the number of bad permutations is even. To do this, we will use the Inclusion-Exclusion principle. Define  $$ Q=\{(a,b,c,d):ad=bc:1\leq a<b<c<d\leq n\} $$  For each pair  $(a,b,c,d)\in Q$ , let  $$ S_{a,b,c,d}=\{\sigma\in T:\text{  $\sigma$  swaps  $(a,b)$  and  $(c,d)$ , OR swaps  $(a,c)$  and  $(b,d)$ }\} $$  Obviously the size of  $S_{a,b,c,d}$  and arbitrary union of them are even since the permutations swapping  $(a,b)$  and  $(c,d)$  can be bijectively mapped to those which swaps  $(a,c)$  and  $(b,d)$ . Now notice that a mapping belongs to  $T$  is bad if and only if it belongs to some  $S_{a,b,c,d}$ . Therefore, by inclusion-exclusion principle, the number of bad permutations in  $T$  is equal to the sum of the size of  $S_{a,b,c,d}$  and their unions modulo  $2$ , where the sum runs through all of  $Q$ , which is even and we are done.

We say that a permutation is *good* if it satisfies the hypotheses in the problem, and *bad* otherwise. **Non-involutions do not matter:** Consider a non-involution  $f$  that permutes over  $[n]$ . Then we have \[ \frac{f(i)}{i}=\frac{f(j)}{j} \Leftrightarrow \frac{f^{-1}(f(i))}{f(i)}=\frac{f^{-1}(f(j))}{f(j)}, \] so using an obvious bijection it suffices to focus only on involutions.**Involutions and Matchings:** We can represent a good involution of  $[n]$  as a maximal matching over  $[n]$ , because there is at most one fixed point. We say that a matching is good if its corresponding permutation is good, and bad otherwise. Realize that constructive counting gives us that the number of maximal matchings over  $[n]$  is  $(2\lceil n/2\rceil-1)!!$ , which is odd. 

Label an edge between vertices  $a$  and  $b$  (where  $a<b$ ) with  $a/b$ . Given a matching we say its *friends* are those matchings obtained as follows: for each label  $\lambda$ , we take some pairs of edges (which can be none) with label  $\lambda$  and apply the following operation:

Given edges  $ab$  and  $cd$  with the same label where  $a<b$  and  $c<d$ , interchange  $b$  and  $c$ . **Key Lemma:** The matching corresponding to the permutation  $\sigma$  has an even number of friends (including itself) iff it is bad. 

*Proof:* Fix a label  $\lambda$ , and suppose  $n$  edges have label  $\lambda$ . Select  $k$  disjoint pairs of edges and apply the operation on each pair; the number of ways to do such a swapping is  $\binom{n}{2k} (2k-1)!!$ , so summing over  $k$ , the total number of ways to perform operations on the edges labeled  $\lambda$  is \[\sum_{k \ge 0} \binom{n}{2k} (2k-1)!! \equiv \sum_{k \ge 0} \binom{n}{2k} =2^{n-1} \pmod{2}. \] The LHS of the above equivalence is even if and only if  $n > 1$ , and consequently odd if and only if  $n=1$ . Moreover, the number of friends of the matching corresponding to  $\sigma$  is the product of  $\sum_{k \ge 0} \binom{n}{2k} (2k-1)!!$  over all  $\lambda$  on the labels. Thus, the number of friends of the matching for  $\sigma$  is odd if and only if all of the labels are distinct, or equivalently when  $\sigma$  is good.  $\square$ **Finish:** Let  $G$  be the simple graph with vertices corresponding to all maximal matchings over  $[n]$ , where edges are determined by friendships, and self-loops are deleted. Note that the good matchings are isolated vertices and that the remaining vertices correspond to bad matchings and have odd degree per the Lemma. Delete the isolated vertices to obtain a new graph  $G'$ . Thus, a well-known consequence of the Handshake Lemma implies that there are an even number of vertices corresponding to bad matchings. Since the number of vertices of  $G$  is odd, the number of vertices corresponding to good matchings is odd, and we are done.
